vignette:
She is 21, African, single, and works as a counselor, a role she once believed would help her make sense of pain by giving it language. Before the war, she imagines her life as orderly enough: she had a routine, people who knew her, and a sense that if she did the right things, she could stay safe. That feeling changes in combat, where danger comes quickly and without warning, and where her body learns before her mind does that nothing can be trusted for long.

She describes the first major attack as the moment everything becomes divided into before and after. She remembers the sharp, immediate sounds, the confusion of shouting, and the way her own breathing seemed too loud in her chest. In the middle of the chaos, she is not thinking in full sentences so much as reacting in fragments: get low, stay quiet, don't move, don't be seen. She recalls the smell of dust and smoke, the sting in her eyes, and the sickening awareness that the people around her are also trying not to die. When she speaks about it now, she still goes distant at certain details, as if she is trying to look at the event from far away because standing inside it feels unbearable.

After that day, fear becomes a constant companion. At first she expects the intensity to fade once the immediate danger passes, but instead her body remains tense, ready for another strike. Sleep comes in short stretches, and even then it is light, broken by sudden waking. She startles at raised voices, slamming doors, and unexpected movement. In crowded places her eyes keep scanning exits, rooftops, and hands. She sits with her back against walls whenever she can, because open space makes her feel exposed. She notices that her muscles never fully unclench and that her jaw aches from holding herself so tightly.

There are nights when the memories come back uninvited. A smell, a sound, or even a certain angle of light can pull her back into the attack with such force that she feels she is there again. She says that during these moments her heart races, her hands shake, and her mind fills with images she cannot stop. Sometimes she wakes with a gasp, reaching for a weapon that is no longer in her hands. Other times she avoids sleep altogether, not because she is not tired, but because she dreads what her mind will do in the dark. She tries to bury the images, but the more she pushes them away, the more insistently they return.

She also becomes quieter around other people. Once, as a counselor, she could sit with someone else's pain and stay present. Now she finds herself pulled inward, listening to clients while also checking the room, tracking her own pulse, and fighting the urge to leave. She still shows up for work, because she believes responsibility is the only thing that keeps her from falling apart, but the effort it takes is exhausting. After sessions she sometimes sits in her car before driving home, unable to move right away. She tells herself to be professional, to stay composed, yet she feels detached from the warmth and ease she used to have with others. Even with friends, she keeps conversations superficial, afraid that if she lets anyone too close they will see how thin her control really is.

She carries guilt that is hard to explain to others. She wonders why she lived when others did not, and why she was frightened when she thinks she should have been stronger. At times she feels ashamed of how much she avoids reminders of combat, even though she knows avoidance is the only way she can get through certain days. She notices that she is more irritable now, less patient with noise, with questions, with delays. Small frustrations can feel enormous. When she is alone, she sometimes stares for long periods, numb and disconnected, as if part of her remains in the past while the rest of her tries to continue forward.

What stands out most is how hard she works to appear steady. She is young, intelligent, and outwardly composed, but beneath that she lives with a body that never fully relaxes and a mind that keeps returning to danger. She moves through her days with discipline, yet every ordinary task requires her to negotiate with memories that still feel immediate, as though the war has not ended so much as followed her home.
